brief.head: Africa next door
brief.text: Most Indians live in conditions comparable to sub-Saharan Africa, Amit Varma said. The people elites think of as chauffeurs and domestic help are the real middle class. {054-C03}

brief.head: English, the network
brief.text: Parents wanted English even when government schools insisted on the vernacular, Ajay Shah said, because it is India’s link language. “The most powerful network of India is English.” {054-C08}

brief.head: A hole in the heart
brief.text: Some people are electrical engineers at work and medieval the rest of the time, Ajay Shah said. A full person brings general intelligence to everything, dahi included. {054-C16}

brief.head: A thousand flowers
brief.text: Ajay Shah wants every IIT, IIM and NIT freed from New Delhi’s central control, which makes them all alike, like public sector banks. “We need a thousand flowers to bloom.” {054-C19}

brief.head: Act in haste
brief.text: A bias for action helps a creator learn by doing, Amit Varma said. For a state wielding coercive power, Ajay Shah argued, it is the greatest enemy. {054-C21}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s broken classrooms
lead.head: Spend more, learn less
body: Almost everyone agrees India needs more: more public and philanthropic money, more teachers, more schools. Ajay Shah said at the outset that he hoped to leave listeners with “a little more disquiet”.
Amit Varma put the alternative in a line. “It’s not about more, it’s about better,” he said. {054-C01}

The evidence of failure is stark. In Aser’s 2022 survey, Varma said, 57 per cent of children in class five could not read a class two text. Among 14 to 18-year-olds, half could not do class three division.

Pouring in money has not helped. Citing Karthik Muralidharan’s research, Varma said that spending more on buildings and toilets, on hiring “better” teachers, or on school bags and midday meals does nothing for learning outcomes.
The trouble is incentives. A teacher works hard until made permanent, he said, and then stops showing up: absenteeism in government schools is “sky high”.

Shah wants every debate to set two numbers side by side: per pupil expense, which has doubled and quadrupled, and an outcome measure such as Aser or PISA. “The first step of the journey of change, of the road to change, is data,” he said. {054-C02}
## Parents vote with their feet

The poor have already given their verdict. Shah said parents are choosing to pay perhaps Rs 4,000 a year for a budget private school rather than take a free government school that spends around Rs 10,000 per pupil.

Varma’s answer is school vouchers, an idea he credited to Milton Friedman: keep the public money, but let it follow the child to any school. “Don’t send it to the schools, give it to the parents,” he said. {054-C06}
Shah took a milder line. Leave government schools as they are, he said, but spend the same on every child in India, whichever school they attend.
## The schooling paradox

Then came a counterintuitive turn. Shah called Lant Pritchett’s *Where Has All the Education Gone?* one of the most important papers in the history of development economics. Across countries and decades, it found the gain in growth from more schooling “essentially zero”. {054-C09}

Shah offered three explanations: failed implementation, education as mere signalling, or a mistaken idea of what education is. Varma backed the third: schools, he said, are “a 19th century machine designed to solve a problem of the 21st century”.
Industrial schooling, Shah argued, nurtures only conscientiousness. “The kids that take orders, the kids who will obey are the ones who will flourish in the industrialised education system,” he said.
## Start at home

What matters most, the hosts agreed, happens before school and outside it. Shah cited James Heckman, whose research finds the best returns in early childhood, from birth to three or five, especially for disadvantaged children. {054-R12}
Much of that learning comes from overhearing adults talk about ideas with a rich vocabulary, Shah said. Varma added that what is missed in those years cannot be made up later.
Parents, Shah argued, should see school for what it is: “a daycare”, just as college is “daycare for teenagers”.
He urged the young to shun credentialism, policymakers to be sceptical of education spending and competitive exams, and philanthropists to fund data and research, as with Aser.
Varma summed up what any learner, of any age, needs. “The key skill in modern times is learning how to learn,” he said.

second.label: Literacy and wealth
second.head: A report card for Nehru
second.deck: Ajay Shah imagines telling Jawaharlal Nehru what seventy-five per cent literacy bought India
body: Jawaharlal Nehru’s generation looked at Britain, with its schools and its Oxford and Cambridge, and saw education as central to development. At independence, Ajay Shah said, female literacy in India was about 6 per cent. {#literacy6}

So Shah imagined going back to Nehru in a time machine and telling him that by 2024 India had about 75 per cent literacy. Nehru, he said, would assume India must be at 60 or 70 per cent of Britain’s per capita GDP. {054-S07}
Instead, Shah said, we would have to hang our heads in shame and admit that India is a lower-middle-income country at a tenth of the global frontier. The literacy came; the rest didn’t happen.

quote.text: if you went back to Jawaharlal Nehru in a time machine and said, 2024 we got like seventy-five percent literacy in India.

second.caption: Nehru in a time machine

third.head: The test India ran from
body: India’s education bureaucracy long resisted the OECD’s PISA test, Ajay Shah said. That is par for the course for a state that likes to control power and money without being accountable for outcomes.
Under international pressure it allowed a little testing, and chose Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, “hoping that it would make India look good. And it didn’t.” {054-S03}
Their 15-year-olds came out among the worst in the world. As Shah remembers it, the bureaucracy then ran away from the project and stopped measuring. “So a cover up was pulled off,” he said.

There was one redeeming feature, an “upper tail bump” of remarkably high scorers. Multiplied by India’s cohort of 15-year-olds, it suggests the second or third largest plausible scientific and engineering workforce in the world. {054-S04} The mainline, Shah said, is horrible.
third.caption: India’s PISA retreat

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Class five, reading class two
sections.caption: the state of Indian schooling
body: Every Indian knows intuitively that the school system is a mess, Amit Varma said. What has changed in the twenty years he has been writing about it is that there is now quality data, and it says things are as bad as ever, or a little worse.
In Aser’s 2022 survey, he said, 57 per cent of class five children could not read a class two text. {#aser57} For them, much of what is taught is “gobbledygook”.
## Where the money goes
The usual remedy is to pump in more money. The Indian state already spends about three per cent of GDP on education, Varma said, mostly on salaries and buildings. {#gdp}

Yet Karthik Muralidharan’s findings, he said, show that better buildings, more toilets, “better” teachers and inputs such as school bags do nothing for outcomes. Midday meals help in many other ways, but not with learning.
The reason is the design of the state. People put in the effort until they are made permanent, Varma said, and “then they are chilling”. {#chilling}

Ajay Shah’s remedy begins with measurement. Per pupil expense, government spending divided by children in government schools, has doubled and quadrupled while outcomes have not improved. Without data, he said, “you can just thrash around for decades”. {054-C02}
~ Speaking as “a good orthodox ex-Ministry of Finance person”, Shah said the country would have done better by taking all that money and paying down debt. {054-J03}

quote.text: Fifty-seven per cent of kids in class five don’t understand what’s going on in class two.

sections.label: Private enterprise
sections.head: Profit, that dirty word
sections.caption: budget private schools
body: Jawaharlal Nehru famously told JRD Tata not to speak to him of profit, as it was a dirty word. That attitude, Amit Varma said, lies behind the rule that schools cannot be run for profit. {054-J12}
The rule, Varma said, came from a misunderstanding of the profit motive: “in a competitive marketplace you earn a profit by serving something, in this case, serving better education.” {054-C04}
Then came licences, which Varma vaguely remembers numbering some forty-two to open a school in Delhi, and utopian rules on playground sizes and toilets. {#licences}
## The poor choose to pay

The poor pay anyway. James Tooley and Pauline Dixon found that many slum dwellers in Hyderabad chose budget private schools over free government ones. {054-R05} A Centre for Civil Society survey of poor Delhi households found the same.
Outcomes, Varma said, are about the same or a little better in private schools, while government schools spend three times as much per student. And parents can demand answers: “Where is a teacher?”
~ Varma’s model is 1991, when markets were let into airlines and telecom and access exploded. His plea, he said, is not to privatise everything, but to stop constraining private players.

quote.text: Every parent wants their child to do better than they themselves did to have opportunities they never had.

sections.label: The voucher
sections.head: Let the money follow the child
sections.caption: school vouchers
body: If the state will spend the money anyway, Amit Varma asked, how can it spend it better? His answer is to fund schooling, not schools, through vouchers, an idea first proposed by Milton Friedman. {054-C06}

Parents would get a voucher worth what the state spends per child, to cash at any school, government or private. Schools would then compete for students, and a teacher who stays absent might find there is no job next year.
Varma’s libertarian friends say the state should spend nothing at all. His reply: don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
## Fairness per child
Ajay Shah went milder. Poor parents, he said, pay perhaps Rs 4,000 a year of their own money to leave a free government school spending about Rs 10,000 per pupil. {054-C05}
Let government schools carry on, he said, but do not abandon the children who leave. “Public spending should be symmetric per child.” {054-C07}
In his advice to policymakers, he rooted this in the Article 14 notion of equality: spend per child in India, not per child in government schools. {#article14}

~ The government schools could become canteens. A bell rings at noon, the children run over for the midday meal, and at 12:45 another bell sends them back. “So this is a great harmonious coexistence,” Shah said. {054-J04}

quote.text: Give it to the parents, let them decide. Let schools then have to compete.

sections.label: Education and growth
sections.head: Schools up, growth flat
sections.caption: Pritchett’s paradox
body: Amit Varma once assumed that a country educates its people first and develops afterwards. When told otherwise, he resisted, until the data changed his mind more than a decade ago.
His friend Murali Neelakantan has mused that the link might run both ways, a virtuous cycle. Not so, Varma said: the cold hard data backs Lant Pritchett. {054-S06}

Ajay Shah set out the evidence. Pritchett’s 2001 paper, *Where Has All the Education Gone?*, was a cold statistical analysis across many countries over long periods. Its answer, he said, was no gain at all. {054-R09}
Pritchett likes to note that Haiti’s education measures today are comparable with France’s in 1970. France then was an extremely developed economy; Haiti is deeply stuck. {054-J13}
## Three suspects

Shah offered three rival explanations. Perhaps implementation failed, which fits India but not the many countries with decent government schools. Perhaps education is mostly signalling, a Louis Vuitton bag. Or perhaps it is defined wrongly, filling the pail instead of kindling the fire.
Varma backed the third. A system that tests a monkey on how to climb a tree, he said, is also testing a fish on how to climb a tree. {054-J15}
~ The truth, Shah said, may lie in all three. Counting learning outcomes instead of inputs explains part of the paradox, but only part.

quote.text: Lant as he does so well was the child saying that the emperor has no clothes, that all this mattered deadly squat.

sections.label: The early years
sections.head: Little ears, big conversations
sections.caption: the first five years
body: James Heckman, the University of Chicago economist, spent his life asking what works, with a hard-nosed eye on return on investment, Ajay Shah said. His answer is early childhood, from birth to three or five, especially for disadvantaged children. {054-R12}

Reading and arithmetic matter, Shah said, and so do social and emotional learning and the regulation of behaviour. From zero to three, he said, a child is adding a million neural connections every second. {054-C12}
## Overheard at home

Much of it comes from overhearing. In a room where adults discuss ideas with a rich vocabulary, Shah said, children are “flapping their ears”. Heckman, half kidding, Shah thinks, once proposed paying starving graduate students to talk to disadvantaged children about ideas. {054-S08}

Family background predicts outcomes as strongly in welfare-state Denmark as in the United States, Shah said. Knowledge flows through families almost unnoticed, which is why populist sneering at nepo babies misses the point. {054-C13}
Amit Varma called it an extra layer of privilege beyond money. Miss those years, he said, and nothing can compensate.
~ Affluent Indian homes, Shah warned, are instead drenched in test prep or mass culture. It was raining on the outdoor shoot, and Varma noted that they too were getting drenched.

quote.text: The family is a site where tremendous intergenerational transformation and knowledge flows take place.

sections.label: Advice to the young
sections.head: Don’t drink the Kool-Aid
sections.caption: credentialism and the young
body: Learning never ends, Ajay Shah said, not at graduation and not at a PhD. For the young, the greatest danger is the Louis Vuitton bag of a famous name: I’m from IIT, so I’m done.
“Don’t drink the Kool-Aid,” he said. Credentialism harms the credentialed first, making them complacent, and then corrupts how they judge everyone else. {054-C18}

Amit Varma added a nuance. Signalling and networks are real, so take the IIT track if it is rational, but don’t be single-track. Immerse in subjects rather than flirting with them. The former cricket journalist has stopped following the game: the IPL, he said, would take his evenings for a month and a half. {054-S12}
## Mixed ages, changed minds
Shah urged people to seek age heterogeneity. At 58, he counts a 25-year-old among the most important people in his life. {054-C14}
And learn to change your mind. Dig in during an argument if you must, he said, but shift your views by five or ten per cent after a week’s reflection. “Actually that’s enough, you’re gold.” {054-C17}
~ Higher up the ladder is thanking the person who changed your mind. Highest of all, Shah said, is saying “I was wrong”.

quote.text: If you’re a twenty-four year old surrounded by twenty-four year olds, you’re doing something wrong.

side.boxText: The OECD’s PISA test, Ajay Shah said, samples 15-year-olds from households, not just schools, and tests whether they can apply science and mathematics, not rote procedures. Finland has the world’s highest scores; South Korea and Japan do very well. {054-R11}

contQuote.text: I think it would be a darn good thing if parents understood that school is a daycare, that college is daycare for teenagers, and no more. So do not confuse school with your education.

p3.title: Tales out of school
p3.deck: Peons, local trains, scooters and orations at home: the stories behind the argument

stories.start: there is this incredible mismatch in the job market where on one hand
stories.end: you can't understand the world. You can't understand text. You're not reading books
stories.caption: the 368 peon jobs
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on degrees without skills
stories.head: The peon jobs PhDs queued for
body: Amit Varma sees the failure of Indian education most clearly in the job market. His friends who run companies tell him they cannot find skilled people, which, he said, is why job-hopping is so common in Bangalore. {#skilled}
Yet the country also has what he called “a crazy unemployment problem”, in which people with the highest degrees are not getting jobs. The two facts sit side by side.

The starkest figure came from Karthik Muralidharan, the guest on a mega episode of Varma’s other show, *The Seen and the Unseen*, who has written a recent book on the Indian state with a good chapter on education.
There had been a recent advertisement, Varma recalled, for 368 government jobs at the level of a peon. About two and a half million people applied, including 250 PhDs. {054-S01}
“Something to that effect,” he added, careful with the figures. By his reckoning it came to some 6,500 applicants for every peon’s post. “This is an incredible crisis.”

It is, Varma said, an illustration of the failure of the education system “all the way through, not just in school”. A lot of degrees, a lot of education all the way up, is “not actually leaving you with any trainable skills”.
~ Nor is the gap only vocational, he insisted. “You can’t understand the world. You can’t understand text. You’re not reading books,” he said. “This is a terrible, terrible problem.”
stories.why: Mass unemployment and a shortage of skills can exist together when degrees are handed out without the abilities they claim to certify. The failure begins early: in class five, most children cannot read a class two text. {#aser57}

stories.start: you can make out from the difference in heights a person's social class
stories.end: What is unseen is what the lack of education also does to people
stories.caption: heights in Bombay’s local trains
stories.head: First class, and a head taller
body: In the 1990s, when Amit Varma came to Bombay, he travelled by local train, and what he saw there was heartbreaking.
People in first class were, on average, significantly taller than people in second class. A lifetime of different nutrition had written social class onto their bodies. {054-S02}

The hosts had lamented before, Varma said, that in India you can make out a person’s social class from their height. {#heights} But height can be seen. “That is visible, that is a seen,” he said. “What is unseen is what the lack of education also does to people.”
~ The difference in cognitive level, he said, is often stark. And that, he added, is a terrible tragedy.

quote.text: it was heartbreaking to see that the people in first class were on average significantly taller than the people in second class.

stories.start: I want to close with uh a story Josh Felman told me
stories.end: articulating it as a 10-20 minute oration. Now that's a high development of capability
stories.caption: Josh Felman’s theory
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah relays a theory from Josh Felman
stories.head: A pulpit in every home
body: Ajay Shah once asked Josh Felman why Jews have such outsized intellectual achievements, including the highest number of Nobel laureates per capita. {054-S09}

The standard answer is selection. In every generation there was a pogrom, Shah said, and the people with portable human capital could up and move and flourish, while those who held land and physical businesses did not survive as well.

Felman offered a different explanation. In the religious meeting, held at home rather than in a formal institution, it is not a priest who gives the oration. The people do, each taking a turn at a 10 to 15-minute talk that ties their personal life to timeless principles.
~ “Every single person who went through that religious tradition was pushing on this ability,” Shah said. “Now that’s a high development of capability.”
stories.why: When a culture makes every ordinary member synthesise ideas out loud, it builds capability at scale. Shah praised serious book clubs; Amit Varma recalled the Takshashila Institution’s Thursday ritual, where researchers present what they learned that week. {054-S10}

stories.start: in the nineteen eighties, I think of airlines. Airlines were prohibitively expensive
stories.end: MTNL, BSNL, whatever the state telecom operators are are essentially irrelevant
stories.caption: flights and phones before 1991
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on planes and phones before 1991
stories.head: Daughter born? Book the scooter
body: Amit Varma is the son of an IAS officer, yet he cannot recall taking a domestic flight as a child in the 1980s. “It was too much even for us,” he said. {054-S05}

The family flew only on a foreign holiday every three years or so. A phone line took five or six years. The joke, he recalled, was that when your daughter is born you book a scooter, so that for her marriage it will be ready. {054-J05}
After the 1991 reforms let markets in, flights and phones became widely accessible. Anybody can now get a phone in five minutes, he said, and MTNL and BSNL are essentially irrelevant.
~ In education, which matters most, India never let markets in, Varma said.
stories.why: Where markets were allowed, access exploded. Varma does not want to privatise everything, he said, only to “just allow private forces to get into play and then see how things turn out”.
